title: Edith Stein (1891–1942)
hook: a Jewish philosopher becomes a Carmelite nun, and is murdered at Auschwitz with her sister

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kolbe before Auschwitz, and the Militia Immaculatae he began: a friar with printing presses and a magazine for Mary. Your line was the knight. Did something good travel through your phone? Today, another name tied to that same camp. Day nine hundred eight.

A borrowed book, read through the night. The reader is a young philosopher, brilliant, Jewish by birth, and for years she has called herself an unbeliever. She's staying at a friend's house, picks up the life of Teresa of Ávila, the Spanish Carmelite, and doesn't put it down. Tradition says that when she closed it at dawn, she said: this is the truth. Edith Stein's mother kept the Jewish faith, and her daughter's choice would cost them both a great deal. Today is her road, from the lecture hall to the convent to a train going east.
screen: `A BOOK READ THROUGH THE NIGHT.` → `THIS IS THE TRUTH.` → `LECTURE HALL, CONVENT, TRAIN.`

segments.voice: Four stops on her road. First, the thinker. She studied philosophy in Germany and worked closely with Edmund Husserl, whose way of thinking, called phenomenology, looks carefully at experience itself. Her doctoral work was on empathy, how one person can truly feel into another's life. Second, the convert. After that night with Teresa, she asked for baptism and was received into the Catholic Church. She taught and lectured, until the Nazi laws pushed Jewish teachers out of their posts. Third, the Carmelite. She entered Carmel in Cologne and took a new name: Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. Teresa, after the book. Benedicta, blessed. And of the cross, because she believed she was being drawn into Christ's suffering, alongside her own people's. Saint Paul writes in Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Her sisters moved her to a Carmel in the Netherlands for safety. Fourth, the train. In the Netherlands, she and her sister Rosa, also a Catholic convert, were arrested and sent to Auschwitz, where they were murdered. They were killed because they were born Jewish. The Church honors her as a saint and a martyr. Some Jewish voices have asked that her story never blur that fact, and that her death be remembered with the death of her people. Both things are true of her.
screen: `THE PHILOSOPHER OF EMPATHY.` · `BAPTIZED AFTER ONE BOOK.` · `TERESA BENEDICTA OF THE CROSS.` · `KILLED BECAUSE SHE WAS BORN JEWISH.` · then, large: `SAVE IN THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Jewish victims of the Holocaust, or hold them in silence. Settle, and breathe. Let Edith and Rosa stand for a moment in your mind, two sisters on one train. Then widen it: the families on that train, and on the others, with names and kitchens and jokes and recipes. You don't need to imagine the horror. Just hold the people. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words. If you don't, simply keep the silence for them. The bell holds the time.
Edith Stein. A Jewish philosopher of empathy who became a Carmelite nun, and was murdered at Auschwitz with her sister Rosa.
Your line: teresa benedicta of the cross. Today, practice her subject: empathy. Listen to one person long enough to feel your way into their day. Day nine hundred eight.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross in August, and she is honored as one of the patron saints of Europe; Carmelites read her writings on the cross.
